area: Area VII. Emergencies and Accident Reporting
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state the PIC's emergency authority and the reports that may follow it, declare a distress or urgency condition with the right words, code and frequency, and name the help ATC, FSS and airport rescue crews can give you.
why: The AIM is blunt: delay in asking for help has caused accidents and cost lives. Many pilots know MAYDAY and 7700 but hesitate to use them, often because they fear the paperwork or the attention. This lesson shows how wide your emergency authority is, how small the reporting burden really is, and how much help is waiting on the other end of the radio.

prereading.what: The PIC's final authority, the emergency deviation power and the written report the FAA may ask for.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.3

prereading.what: Deviating from an ATC clearance or instruction in an emergency, telling ATC, and the 48 hour priority report.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.123

prereading.what: Pilot authority, and why an urgency condition starts the moment you become doubtful.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-1 to 6-1-2

prereading.what: Radar help for VFR pilots in difficulty, transponder emergency operation, and intercept and escort.
prereading.label: AIM 6-2-1 to 6-2-3

prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1 to 6-3-2

warmup: Think first: you are VFR at 4,500 ft, talking to approach for flight following on code 4721. The low fuel light for the left tank comes on, you are not sure the right tank reading is right, and the field you planned is 35 minutes away. Nothing has failed yet. Is this an emergency? Would you say MAYDAY, PAN-PAN, "minimum fuel," or nothing? Would you change your squawk? Write your answers down, then check them at the end of chunk 4.

key_terms.def: A distress or an urgency condition (Pilot/Controller Glossary).
Being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and needing immediate assistance. Signal: MAYDAY.
Being concerned about safety and needing timely but not immediate assistance; a potential distress condition. Signal: PAN-PAN.
The 91.3(b) power of the PIC, in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, to deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required.
A new clearance you ask for after deviating from the old one, so ATC and you share the same plan again.
An advisory that you can accept little or no delay at destination. It is not an emergency and does not ask for priority.
Fuel stated as the approximate number of minutes you can keep flying, counting all reserve fuel.
The transponder emergency code. It normally sets off an alarm or special indicator at every control position of a radar facility.
The civil emergency frequency. Line of sight, and guarded by direction finding stations, most civil towers, radar facilities and some aircraft.
A way for a ground facility to find your bearing from your radio transmissions, used to help lost pilots.
Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting Incident Commander. Called on the radio as "(location) Command."
A frequency ATC designates so the flight crew, the ARFF IC and the tower can talk directly.

callout.text: 91.3: the pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required to meet that emergency. A PIC who deviates must send a written report of the deviation to the Administrator, upon request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

body.p: Read the three limits built into paragraph (b). It is for an in-flight emergency. The emergency must require immediate action. And the deviation goes only as far as the emergency requires [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. The power is wide: any rule of part 91 [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. Interpretation: that reaches weather minimums, altitudes, airspace and clearances alike.

The AIM restates the rule and adds the follow-up: if you use 91.3(b) to deviate from an ATC clearance, notify ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1b]]. The AIH says flight instructors should teach that declaring an emergency when one occurs is an appropriate reaction, and that ATC then gives priority handling [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

callout.text: Wording note: AIM 6-1-1a says the PIC may deviate from any rule in 14 CFR part 91, Subpart A and Subpart B [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. The regulation the AIM cites says any rule of this part [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. The CFR is the rule, so this lesson teaches the CFR wording.

body.p: Interpretation: 91.3(b) is not a license to break unrelated rules once an emergency is declared. A rough engine justifies flying below a minimum altitude to reach a field; it does not justify skipping a clearance you had time to request.

check.q: What three conditions does 91.3(b) put on an emergency deviation?
check.a: An in-flight emergency, requiring immediate action, and only to the extent required to meet it [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]].

chunks.title: Clearances, instructions and the reports that may follow

body.p: 91.123 ties the emergency power to ATC. With a clearance, you may not deviate unless you get an amended clearance, an emergency exists, or you are following a TCAS resolution advisory [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. Except in an emergency, you may not operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]].

head: After the emergency
To whom
When
Source
rows: You deviated from a clearance or instruction
Get back on the same plan as ATC
You deviated from a part 91 rule under 91.3(b)
ATC gave you priority, even with no rule broken
Manager of that ATC facility, a detailed report
Within 48 hours, only if ATC requests it
The event was an accident or a listed serious incident

callout.text: Memory aid (our own, not FAA): "Tell now, write if asked." Telling ATC is required as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]; the written reports happen only on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

body.p: Interpretation: declaring an emergency does not by itself trigger a report. The two written reports in part 91 are both on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]], and the NTSB call depends on what happened, not on whether you declared [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

check.q: ATC gave you priority for a rough-running engine and you broke no rule. What report could you owe, and to whom?
check.a: A detailed report of the emergency within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility, but only if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

chunks.title: Distress, urgency, or just an advisory?

head: Condition
What it means
How you say it
Source
rows: Threatened by serious and/or imminent danger, needing immediate assistance
MAYDAY, three times: imminent and grave danger, immediate assistance requested
Concerned about safety, needing timely but not immediate assistance; a potential distress condition
PAN-PAN, three times: uncertainty or alert, then the nature of the urgency
You can accept little or no undue delay at destination. Not an emergency, and it does not ask for priority
Call sign, then "minimum fuel" on initial contact

body.p: An emergency is either a distress or an urgency condition [[34:340|P/CG E-1]]. The AIM's key line: an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or any other condition that could adversely affect flight safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

callout.text: If your remaining usable fuel suggests you need traffic priority to land safely, declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]. "Minimum fuel" never buys priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

bullets: Distress examples the AIM gives: fire, mechanical failure, structural damage [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
A noninstrument rated pilot who can no longer continue in VFR conditions should tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]].

The AFH says a VFR pilot who cannot keep attitude control by the natural horizon, or cannot fix position by landmarks on the ground, is in effect in IMC, and should treat it as a genuine emergency requiring appropriate action [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: You are not sure where you are and your fuel is getting low, but the engine runs fine. Which condition are you in?
check.a: At least urgency. Doubt about position or fuel endurance puts you there, and that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

chunks.title: Making the call: MAYDAY, PAN-PAN and the message

body.p: You can get help informally, by telling the facility you are talking to what the problem is, what you intend and what help you want. The ICAO procedures have decided advantages over that [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]: start the first call, and later calls if needed, with MAYDAY for distress or PAN-PAN for urgency, preferably three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

bullets: MAYDAY gets absolute priority and commands radio silence on the frequency. PAN-PAN has priority over everything except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

Call the facility you are already working, on that frequency. If you are not talking to anyone, call the facility responsible for your area. If no one answers, or time is short, broadcast to "Any Station" [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

The station that hears you acknowledges, helps, coordinates other facilities and alerts search and rescue if warranted. Other stations keep listening and step in if the first station cannot reach you [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

body.p: Send as many of these elements as needed, preferably in this order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. Fuel goes in minutes. The glossary says to state the approximate number of minutes you can keep flying, with all reserve fuel included and an allowance for gauge error [[34:349|P/CG F-6]].

callout.text: Application: the first four items (signal, station, call sign and type, nature of the problem) get help moving. If the airplane needs your hands, fly first and add the rest later; the AIM asks only for as many elements as necessary [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

body.p: After contact, comply with advice and instructions, cooperate, and ask when you do not understand or cannot comply. Help keep the frequency quiet. Do not change frequency unless you must; if you do, tell the station first, and if the new frequency fails, go back to the last one that worked [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]].

check.q: Warm-up answer: low fuel light on, unsure of the other tank, 35 minutes to go, talking to approach. What do you say?
check.a: At least urgency, since you doubt your fuel endurance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]: "PAN-PAN" three times, then the message, with fuel in minutes [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. If you think you will need priority to land safely, declare an emergency for low fuel; "minimum fuel" does not get priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]. Keep code 4721 while you are talking to approach (chunk 5).

chunks.title: Squawk 7700, 121.5, and climbing to be heard

head: Your situation
Transponder
Source
rows: In radio contact with ATC on an assigned code
Keep the assigned code and Mode C unless told otherwise
Not in contact: you cannot immediately establish communications, or you want to alert a radar facility before you call
7700 and Mode C, then establish communications as soon as possible
Air piracy or hostile act aboard
7500, if you cannot give the information by voice

body.p: When a controller says "squawk Mayday," set the emergency code 7700 [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]]. 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all control positions. You may be outside radar coverage, so keep squawking 7700 and keep trying the radio [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. Emergency autoland systems set 7700 and broadcast on 121.5 MHz on their own [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

bullets: The frequency in use or one ATC assigned is preferred. 121.5 MHz is there if necessary or desirable [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
121.5 is line of sight. It is guarded by direction finding stations, some military and civil aircraft, military towers, most civil towers and radar facilities [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
ARTCC emergency frequency coverage normally does not reach the edge of its radar coverage. If Center does not answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Climb if possible, for better communications, radar and DF detection. Under IFR in controlled airspace an unauthorized climb or descent is prohibited, except as 91.3(b) permits [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2a1]].

callout.text: The PHAK gives the same order for a lost VFR pilot: climb for radio, navigation and radar reception, call any facility shown on the sectional, and if it gets threatening, transmit on 121.5 and set 7700 [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

check.q: On flight following with a discrete code, your oil pressure starts dropping. Do you switch to 7700?
check.a: Not unless told to. In radio contact, keep the assigned code and Mode C; 7700 is for when you cannot immediately establish communications [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

chunks.title: Help in the air: radar, DF, FSS and escort

body.p: Help is available from radio, radar, direction finding stations and other aircraft [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Here is what each one can do.

head: Service
What you get
Source
rows: Radar assistance to VFR aircraft in difficulty
Radar assistance and vectors, if you can talk to the controller and are in radar coverage. Vectors are advisory; flying safely stays your job
The controller asks you to key the mike for a few seconds, maybe after a few heading changes, to plot your position and give vectors to a landing site
Search and rescue services, and assistance to lost aircraft and aircraft in emergency situations

A search and rescue aircraft joins you, helps in flight and escorts you to a safe landing. Provided if you ask for it or declare distress; may be started for urgency when unusual circumstances make it advisable
ARTCCs and FSSs alert the SAR system when they learn an aircraft is in difficulty, overdue or missing

body.p: Many FSSs transmit through Remote Communications Outlets. The chart shows the frequencies above the communications box; tell the specialist your location and the frequency you are listening on, so the right transmitter answers [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a2]]. On the chart legend, frequencies above a thin line box are remoted to that site, and other FSS frequencies may be available depending on altitude and terrain [[2:26|CUG 26]].

bullets: You may refuse intercept and escort. Escort normally goes to the nearest adequate airport; if you go elsewhere, further escort is up to the escort [[34:30|AIM 6-2-3c]].
Radar facilities giving flight following treat loss of radar and radio without a service termination notice as a possible emergency, and SAR may start [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]].

Use ATC services you can reach. Radar facilities provide safety alerts, traffic advisories and limited vectoring when requested to VFR aircraft that can communicate and are in radar coverage [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]].

check.q: Approach is giving you vectors toward an airport. If the vector would take you into cloud, whose problem is that?
check.a: Yours. Radar navigational guidance is advisory, responsibility for flying safely stays with the pilot, and it is not authorization to violate the CFRs [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Keep the controller told about the weather you see [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]].

chunks.title: Help on the ground: rescue crews and how to talk to them

body.p: When a landing gear malfunction makes a gear-up landing inevitable, the AFH says to pick an airport with crash and rescue facilities if possible, and not to hesitate to ask that emergency equipment stand by [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]. Application: the same request makes sense for any landing you expect may end badly.

bullets: At a towered airport, ATC can designate a Discrete Emergency Frequency so you, the ARFF Incident Commander and the tower can talk directly [[34:56|AIM 6-5-1]].
With no tower, or the tower closed, call the ARFF IC (if the airport has ARFF) on the CTAF or on 121.5 MHz [[34:56|AIM 6-5-1]].
The ARFF IC's call sign is "(location or facility) Command," for example "LAX Command" [[34:56|AIM 6-5-2]].
If radio contact with the IC is lost, standard hand signals are used, and the AIM says all cockpit and cabin crew should know them [[34:56|AIM 6-5-3]].

body.p: This signal means the IC, looking at the outside of your airplane, recommends evacuation [[34:56|AIM 6-5-3]]. The AIM shows two more: recommend stop, and emergency contained [[34:57|AIM 6-5-3]].

callout.text: Application: before a planned emergency landing, brief your passengers on the evacuation signal and on how to open the doors, so the fire crew's gesture means something to everyone aboard.

check.q: You are inbound with smoke to a nontowered airport that has ARFF. How do you reach the incident commander?
check.a: On the CTAF published for the airport or on 121.5 MHz [[34:56|AIM 6-5-1]], calling "(airport name) Command" [[34:56|AIM 6-5-2]].

chunks.title: Risk: waiting too long to declare

body.p: Pilots declare quickly for fire or a failed engine. They hesitate when the danger is not immediate but could become catastrophic. The AIM says the time to ask for help is then, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. The IPH puts the same point plainly: request assistance when an urgent situation may have, or has just, occurred [[29:287|IPH A-1]].

head: What pilots tell themselves
What the sources say
rows: Doubt about position, fuel endurance or weather is already at least urgency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
Both part 91 reports are only on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].
Declaring brings additional assistance and priority handling [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. AC 91-92 lists hesitating to declare when safety is at risk as a "don't" [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].
Too many situations that call for a precautionary landing turn into forced landings when the pilot uses wishful thinking instead of reason [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
An airplane not certificated for icing should exit the conditions as quickly as possible and declare an emergency to ATC [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]].

body.p: The AFH names the psychological traps: reluctance to accept the situation, which brings indecision and delay; fear that turns to panic; and the desire to save the airplane, pushed by the pilot's financial stake [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: The AIM: pilots who become apprehensive for their safety for any reason should request assistance immediately. Delay has caused accidents and cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

Application: set a personal trigger before you fly, for example "if I am not sure of my position and fuel at the same time, I call PAN-PAN." A rule made on the ground is easier to follow than a decision made while scared.

check.q: Which AFH psychological hazard shows up as indecision and delay in picking a landing area?
check.a: Reluctance to accept the emergency situation [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

chunks.title: Fly it: working an emergency with ATC

body.p: Example: alternator failure. The AFH treats any loss of electrical power in a small airplane as critical: shed everything but the most necessary equipment, notify ATC immediately, and ask for radar vectors to the nearest suitable airport [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

The table shows why load shedding matters. Pitot heat, lights and radios draw continuously, while landing lights, the flap motor and the gear motor draw big currents in short bursts [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. A 25 amp-hour battery might give 5 amps for 5 hours, but a 10 amp load might last only 2 hours, and a 40 amp load might drain it in about 10 or 15 minutes [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Electric flaps and gear may not work on a partly drained battery and can cause a total power loss; plan a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

head: Step
What you do
Source
rows: Keep control first. The AFH warns against desperate attempts to fix the problem at the expense of airplane control
Distress or urgency; doubt alone is urgency
MAYDAY or PAN-PAN three times, then the message elements as needed
Keep the assigned code in contact; 7700 if you cannot reach anyone
Vectors, DF, FSS, escort; application: ask for rescue equipment standing by
Tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance
7. If landing off airport is imminent
Add ELT status, landmarks, aircraft color, persons and emergency equipment aboard; activate the ELT if you can

callout.text: ATC may sound rushed when giving headings and altitudes. That is normal concern for safety, but do not let it hurry you into a maneuver that could cost control. It is reasonable to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

body.p: If the radios fail instead, whether that is an emergency is your call, and 91.3(b) is there if the situation needs it [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], and try the last frequency, an FSS, or 121.5, all at once if you can [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3]]. IFR lost communications rules ([[60:482|14 CFR 91.185]]) are in RF.V.C.

check.q: Alternator failed, battery only. Which two loads in AFH Figure 18-9 should you most avoid using on a partly drained battery?
check.a: The flap motor and the landing gear motor. They draw far more than most equipment and may cause an immediate total loss of power [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

head: Error
Fix
Source
rows: Waiting for the situation to become obvious
Call at the first doubt; that is already urgency
Saying "minimum fuel" when you need priority
Declare an emergency for low fuel and give fuel in minutes
Giving fuel in gallons, or subtracting reserve
Give approximate minutes of flight, with reserve fuel included
Switching to 7700 while working ATC on a discrete code
Keep the assigned code unless told otherwise
Changing frequency in the middle of the emergency
Stay put unless you must; tell the station first
Following a vector into cloud as a VFR-only pilot
Choose the VFR option, keep ATC told of the weather, and declare distress if VFR is no longer possible
Forgetting to tell ATC after a deviation
Notify as soon as possible and get an amended clearance
Turning the emergency over to the airplane's value
Sacrifice the airplane if that lets people walk away

callout.text: Memory aid (our own, not FAA): "Fly, Name, Call, Squawk, Use." Fly the airplane, name the condition, make the call, set the right code, use every service offered [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]] [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]] [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

check.q: You told ATC "minimum fuel" and now realize you need to land ahead of other traffic. What now?
check.a: Declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes; minimum fuel does not imply traffic priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

f1.caption: AIM 6-1-1 and 6-1-2 (page excerpt, no figure number): Pilot Responsibility and Authority, and Emergency Condition, Request Assistance Immediately (AIM 6-1-1).
f1.alt: Text excerpt from the AIM. Paragraph 6-1-1 says the pilot in command is the final authority and may deviate in an emergency, must notify ATC and get an amended clearance after deviating from a clearance, and IFR pilots with radio failure follow 91.185. Paragraph 6-1-2 defines emergency as distress or urgency, says an aircraft is in at least urgency when the pilot becomes doubtful, and ends: Safety is not a luxury! Take action!

f2.alt: A list of eleven message elements, (a) to (k): MAYDAY or PAN-PAN three times; name of station addressed; aircraft identification and type; nature of distress or urgency; weather; pilot's intentions and request; present position and heading, or if lost, last known position, time and heading since; altitude or flight level; fuel remaining in minutes; number of people on board; any other useful information.

f5.alt: Table of electrical loads for a light single. Continuous load: pitot heating 3.30 amps, four wingtip lights 3.00, heater igniter 1 to 20, navigation receivers and communications receivers 1 to 2 each, fuel indicator 0.40, two instrument lights 0.60, engine indicator 0.30, compass light 0.20, landing gear and flap indicators 0.17 each. Intermittent load: starter 100.00, two landing lights 17.80, heater blower motor 14.00, flap motor 13.00, landing gear motor 10.00, cigarette lighter 7.50, keyed transceiver 5 to 7, fuel boost pump 2.00, cowl flap motor 1.00, stall warning horn 1.50. A note says panel and indicator lights usually draw less than one amp.

Text beside it explains the signal is based on the ARFF incident commander's assessment of the outside situation, and that at night the same signal is made with wands.

scenario.title: Dark panel over the lake
scenario.setup: You are flying a Piper Archer with steam gauges, one alternator and one battery, VFR at night at 5,500 ft, on flight following with approach on code 3346. A friend is aboard. Over a large lake, 40 miles from home, the low voltage light comes on and the ammeter shows a discharge. Resetting the alternator does not help. A Class C airport with ARFF is 18 miles ahead; your home field, nontowered, is behind you. Your passenger asks, "Do we really have to make a fuss about this?"

questions.q: Is this worth declaring, and how urgent is it?
questions.a: Yes. The AFH says any loss of electrical power is critical in a small airplane and to notify ATC immediately [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. The battery may not last long, especially if the failure was not caught right away [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. At night over water this is at least urgency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]; declaring brings additional assistance and priority [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

questions.q: What do you do with the electrical load before you key the mike for a long call?
questions.a: Shed all but the most necessary equipment [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Application: from AFH Figure 18-9, pitot heat (3.30 A) is an easy cut on a clear night, while the position lights stay on at night. Plan to use landing lights, flaps and the radio sparingly [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

questions.q: What do you say, and do you change your transponder code?
questions.a: "PAN-PAN" three times, the station, call sign and type, the problem, intentions and request, position, altitude, fuel in minutes and persons aboard [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. Keep code 3346 and Mode C, since you are in contact with ATC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

questions.q: Approach offers vectors to the Class C airport and asks if you want the rescue trucks. What help should you accept?
questions.a: Radar vectors to the nearest suitable airport, as the AFH suggests [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]; the vectors are advisory and safe flying stays with you [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Application: ask for emergency equipment standing by, as the AFH advises for a gear-up landing [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]. Plan a no-flap landing, since electric flaps may not work on a weak battery [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

questions.q: The radio dies on final, before you get a landing clearance. You land anyway. What authority covers that, and what follows?
questions.a: 91.3(b) lets you deviate from any part 91 rule to the extent the emergency requires [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]], and 91.123 lets you deviate from an ATC clearance or instruction in an emergency [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]. Notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] (application: by phone after landing, if the radio stays dead). A written report goes to the Administrator only if requested [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]].

questions.q: The next day the tower manager calls and asks for a report. Does anything go to the NTSB?
questions.a: The tower may ask for a detailed report within 48 hours because you were given priority [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]. Nothing goes to the NTSB by these facts. No one was hurt and nothing was damaged, so it is not an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. The electrical failure item in 830.5 covers only large multiengine aircraft over 12,500 pounds [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)(7)]], and the display item covers a complete loss of information from more than 50 percent of EFIS, EICAS, ECAM or similar integrated displays [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5(a)(9)]], which a steam-gauge panel does not have. On a glass panel the same failure could be a listed serious incident (RF.VII.B).

skills.do: Given an emergency (electrical failure, low fuel, lost, smoke, weather), name the condition as distress or urgency, make a clear MAYDAY or PAN-PAN call with the AIM message elements in order, set the right transponder code for whether you are in contact, choose the frequency (current, then 121.5 or the nearest tower), accept and use the services offered, deviate only to the extent required, and say what you must tell ATC afterward and which reports may be requested.
skills.practice: Write a one-line message template on your kneeboard from AIM 6-3-2a3 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]]. With a CFI or a friend acting as ATC, run five emergencies out loud from start to amended clearance, including one where you are not in contact (7700 and 121.5) [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]] [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Then, on a real flight with flight following, practice finding the nearest RCO and tower frequencies on the sectional [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a2]].

quiz.q: Which wording is in the regulation itself, 14 CFR 91.3(b)?
options: The PIC may deviate from any rule in part 91 Subparts A and B, to the extent required
The PIC may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency
The PIC may deviate from any rule of this part for the rest of the flight once an emergency is declared
The PIC may deviate from ATC clearances, but not from other rules
quiz.why: 91.3(b): in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. The Subparts A and B wording is how AIM 6-1-1a states it [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

quiz.q: You set 7700 and call for help, but no one answers. What does the AIM say about the code?
options: Go back to 1200, since no one is watching
Keep squawking 7700 and establish radio contact as soon as possible; you may be outside radar coverage
Switch to 7600, since no one answered
Turn the transponder off to save the battery
quiz.why: 7700 normally triggers an alarm at all control positions, but you might not be in radar coverage, so keep squawking 7700 and establish radio communications as soon as possible [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

quiz.q: Which statement about 121.5 MHz is correct?
options: Its range is generally limited to line of sight
Every ARTCC guards it out to the edge of its radar coverage
You should use it in preference to the frequency you are already on
Only military aircraft guard it
quiz.why: 121.5 and 243.0 have a range generally limited to line of sight. The frequency in use is preferred, ARTCC coverage on 121.5 normally does not reach radar limits, and 121.5 is guarded by DF stations, some aircraft, most civil towers and radar facilities [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

quiz.q: What does a VFR pilot in difficulty need for radar assistance and vectors from ATC?
options: An IFR flight plan
To be able to talk with the controller and to be within radar coverage
A filed VFR flight plan
A MAYDAY call first; PAN-PAN does not qualify
quiz.why: Radar facilities can give radar assistance and vectors to VFR aircraft in difficulty when the pilot can talk with the controller and the aircraft is within radar coverage [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

quiz.q: What does the word PAN-PAN tell other stations on the frequency?
options: To keep radio silence until the frequency is released
Not to interfere with urgency transmissions
That the aircraft has lost two-way radio
That the aircraft is being hijacked
quiz.why: Urgency communications have priority over all but distress, and PAN-PAN warns other stations not to interfere with urgency transmissions. It is MAYDAY that commands radio silence [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

quiz.q: In an emergency, ATC gives you an instruction you cannot comply with. What does the AIM say?
options: Comply anyway, because ATC has priority
Do what you think best and say nothing
Do not hesitate to ask questions or clarify, including when you cannot comply
Squawk 7600 to show you cannot comply
quiz.why: After radio contact, comply with advice and instructions and cooperate, but do not hesitate to ask questions or clarify instructions when you do not understand or cannot comply [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]].

quiz.q: Which service does an FSS provide in an emergency?
options: Separation of VFR traffic
Assistance to lost aircraft and aircraft in emergency situations
ARFF incident command
Clearances into Class B airspace
quiz.why: FSSs provide search and rescue services and assistance to lost aircraft and aircraft in emergency situations [[33:204|AIM 4-1-3]].

quiz.q: What is the preferred radio call sign of the ARFF Incident Commander?
options: "(location) Rescue"
"(location) Command"
"(location) Fire"
"(location) Emergency"

quiz.q: Which AFH psychological hazard is the one where fear can turn into panic?
options: Reluctance to accept the emergency situation
Undue concern about getting hurt
Desire to save the airplane
Wishful thinking about the weather
quiz.why: Under undue concern about getting hurt, the AFH says fear is part of self-preservation, but when it leads to panic it invites what we most want to avoid [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

final_quiz.q: IFR in cloud in controlled airspace, a partial panel failure makes you want better radio and radar coverage higher up, but you have no clearance to climb. What does the AIM say?
options: Climb anyway; the AIM says to climb whenever in difficulty
An unauthorized climb under IFR in controlled airspace is prohibited, except as 91.3(b) permits
Climbs are never allowed without a clearance, even in an emergency
Squawk 7600 and then climb
final_quiz.why: Climb if possible, but an unauthorized climb or descent under IFR conditions in controlled airspace is prohibited except as permitted by 91.3(b) [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2a1]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]].

final_quiz.q: VFR at night over a dark area, you lose the horizon and every ground light, and you can no longer tell where you are by landmarks. How does the AFH say to treat this?
options: As normal night flying, as long as the engine runs
As a genuine emergency requiring appropriate action
As a minimum fuel situation
As something to report only after landing
final_quiz.why: A VFR pilot who cannot keep attitude control by the natural horizon, or cannot fix position by landmarks, is in effect in IMC, and should accept it as a genuine emergency requiring appropriate action [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

final_quiz.q: You are instrument rated and current in an IFR-equipped airplane, VFR, getting radar help as the weather ahead closes in. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Declare distress and say you lack an instrument rating
Request an IFR flight clearance
Squawk 7700 and continue VFR into the clouds
Cancel radar service and turn back on your own
final_quiz.why: If the pilot is instrument rated and current and the aircraft is instrument equipped, the pilot should request an IFR flight clearance; help is then given on the basis that the aircraft can operate safely in IFR conditions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]].

final_quiz.q: On VFR flight following you land at a small field, tie down and go to lunch without telling approach. What may happen?
options: Nothing; VFR services end on their own
Search and rescue may start, since loss of radar and radio without a termination notice is treated as a possible emergency
ATC will cancel your flight plan automatically
You will owe a written report under 91.3(c)
final_quiz.why: Radar facilities giving flight following or advisories treat loss of radar and radios without a service termination notice as a possible emergency, and SAR may be started [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]].

final_quiz.q: You declared an emergency, and to stay clear of cloud you descended below an altitude ATC assigned. What must you do?
options: Nothing until you land
Notify ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance
File a written report within 48 hours
Squawk 7600 to show the deviation
final_quiz.why: Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] and obtain an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1b]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot says that declaring an emergency for a rough engine automatically means an NTSB report. Which is right?
options: True for every declared emergency
True only for MAYDAY, not PAN-PAN
False: NTSB notification depends on whether an accident or a listed serious incident occurred
False: the NTSB is notified only if ATC asks for a report
final_quiz.why: 830.5 requires immediate notification when an aircraft accident or a listed serious incident occurs (or an aircraft is overdue and believed in an accident); a declaration is not on the list [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: VFR, both radios quit. Who decides whether that is an emergency?
options: ATC, once it notices you are not answering
The pilot, depending on the circumstances
No one; radio failure is always an emergency
No one; radio failure is never an emergency
final_quiz.why: Whether two-way communications failure is an emergency depends on the circumstances, and it is a determination made by the pilot [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]].

final_quiz.q: During an emergency, approach asks you to switch to another frequency. The new one is silent. What do you do?
options: Squawk 7700 and stay on the new frequency
Go back immediately to the frequency where two-way contact last existed
Call on 243.0 MHz
Wait 5 minutes and try again
final_quiz.why: If two-way communication cannot be established on the new frequency, return immediately to the frequency or station where it last existed [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]].

final_quiz.q: An SAR aircraft joins you after you declared distress. You decide to continue past the nearest adequate airport to your home field. What happens to the escort?
options: It must stay with you until you land
Further escort is discretionary; it is not obligated to continue
It will order you to land at the nearest airport
You lose your 91.3 authority
final_quiz.why: Escort is normally to the nearest adequate airport; if you go on elsewhere, the escort is not obligated to continue [[34:30|AIM 6-2-3c]]. You may refuse escort altogether [[34:30|AIM 6-2-3c]].

final_quiz.q: Your 25 amp-hour battery is a few years old, and you noticed the low voltage light late. What does the AFH say about its example of 5 amps for 5 hours?
options: It holds for any battery of that rating
Battery age and a failure not caught right away can leave far less energy than the rating suggests
An old battery lasts longer because it is broken in
It applies only to glass-cockpit airplanes
final_quiz.why: Much depends on battery condition: an older battery may have much less power because of internal resistance, and if the failure was not detected immediately, much of the stored energy may already be gone [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

final_quiz.q: After a gear-up landing at a towered airport, fire trucks surround your airplane. Your radio is dead. The incident commander holds one arm out, hand up at eye level, beckoning backward. What does it mean?
options: Stop the engine and stay seated
Emergency contained
Evacuation recommended
Taxi clear of the runway
final_quiz.why: That is the Recommend Evacuation signal, based on the IC's assessment of the outside situation [[34:56|AIM 6-5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Inbound with smoke to a towered airport, you want to talk directly with the fire crew's incident commander. What does the AIM describe?
options: Calling the fire station by cell phone
A Discrete Emergency Frequency, designated by ATC, shared by you, the ARFF IC and the tower
Calling the IC on the ground control frequency without telling the tower
Only hand signals are allowed at towered airports
final_quiz.why: ATC can designate a Discrete Emergency Frequency from its operational frequencies, so the flight crew, the ARFF IC and the tower can talk directly [[34:56|AIM 6-5-1]].

final_quiz.q: In a non-icing-certificated airplane at night you pick up ice, and approach is too busy to give you a new altitude quickly. What does AC 91-74B recommend?
options: Wait for the clearance; deviating is illegal
Declare an emergency and exit the conditions as soon as practical
Squawk 7600 and climb
Cancel flight following and descend without telling anyone
final_quiz.why: If a clearance may not come in time, declare an emergency and exit the conditions as soon as practical [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. 91.123(a) allows deviation when an emergency exists [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

takeaways: 91.3(b): in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action you may deviate from any part 91 rule, but only as far as the emergency requires.
After deviating from a clearance, tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance. Written reports come only if the FAA or ATC asks.
Doubt about position, fuel or weather is already urgency. Ask for help then, not after it becomes distress.
MAYDAY for distress, PAN-PAN for urgency, three times, then as many message elements as needed, with fuel in minutes.
Keep your assigned code while in contact; 7700 when you cannot reach anyone. Use your current frequency first, 121.5 if needed.
Radar vectors, DF, FSS, intercept and escort, and rescue crews standing by are all available. Ask.
"Minimum fuel" is not an emergency and gets no priority. If you need priority, declare.
cfi_notes: AIM 6-1-1a and 6-4-1b say the PIC may deviate from rules in part 91 Subparts A and B [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]] [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]. 91.3(b) says any rule of this part [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. The regulation is the rule, so teach the CFR wording and simply point out the different AIM wording.

Two AIM transponder lines read differently: 6-2-2a says a pilot who wants to alert a ground radar facility should squawk 7700 and then immediately establish communications [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]; 6-3-2a2 says keep the assigned or VFR code while in radio contact unless told otherwise, and squawk 7700 if unable to immediately establish communications [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. Interpretation: together they mean 7700 when you are not yet talking to anyone, and the assigned code once you are in contact. The lesson's questions use only those two clear cases.

Pilots confuse the reports: telling ATC (91.123(c)), the on-request reports (91.3(c), 91.123(d)) and the NTSB call (49 CFR 830.5) [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Use the chunk 2 table, and send them to RF.VII.B for 830.
AC 61-98E lists Authority (91.3) among the flight review items [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]]. A two-minute role play, with you as ATC, tests it better than a definition does.
The P/CG asks pilots to include an allowance for gauge system error in fuel remaining [[34:349|P/CG F-6]] but does not say how. Interpretation: have pilots state what they can actually count on.
RF.IV.C covers clearances and the special codes in general; RF.V.C covers IFR lost communications under 91.185. Here, keep the focus on deciding to declare and using the help.

The AFH's electrical figures (25 amp-hours: 5 amps for 5 hours, but 10 amps might last only 2 hours) show the battery does not scale evenly [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Do not let pilots divide amp-hours by load and trust the answer.
Use the AFH psychological hazards [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[24:351|AFH 18-2]] as discussion prompts: ask the pilot when they last hesitated to tell ATC about a problem, and why.
gaps: The sources do not say what follow-up, if any, the FAA does after a declared emergency with no rule broken, beyond the on-request reports in 91.3(c) and 91.123(d).
Which airports have ARFF, and their Discrete Emergency Frequencies, are in the Chart Supplement, which is not in the sources.
Your airplane's own emergency checklists (electrical, fire, engine) come from the POH/AFM; the AFH guidance is generic and the manufacturer's procedures take precedence [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
How long a given battery lasts after an alternator failure depends on the battery and its age; the AFH gives only rough examples [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].
The sources do not list where direction finding service is available today or how to request it beyond the AIM and PHAK descriptions.

activities.title: Name it right
activities.intro: Tap a term, then its meaning.

pairs.r: Serious or imminent danger; immediate assistance needed
Timely but not immediate assistance; potential distress
Either a distress or an urgency condition
Little or no delay acceptable; not an emergency
Normally sets off an alarm or special indicator at all radar control positions
Uncertainty or alert, then the nature of the urgency
Approximate minutes of flight, reserve included

activities.why: Pilot/Controller Glossary definitions [[34:337|P/CG D-4]] [[34:437|P/CG U-2]] [[34:340|P/CG E-1]] [[34:379|P/CG M-4]] [[34:392|P/CG P-1]] [[34:349|P/CG F-6]], and the AIM on code 7700 [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

activities.title: Build the distress message
activities.intro: Put the AIM's message elements in the preferred order, then tap Check.
activities.why: AIM 6-3-2a3 lists the elements (a) to (k), preferably in this order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

activities.title: Which help fits?
activities.intro: Tap a case, then the service that gives that help.

items.t: Talking to approach, in radar coverage, you want a heading to the nearest airport
Safety alerts and limited vectoring when you ask for them
The controller asks you to hold the mike button down a few seconds, then turn and do it again
A ground station plots your position from your transmissions and gives vectors to a landing site
You declared distress over remote terrain and want an aircraft to join you and stay with you to a landing
Your gear will not come down and you want fire trucks standing by

activities.why: Radar assistance and vectors need two-way radio and radar coverage [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]] [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]]; DF works from your transmissions [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]; SAR intercept and escort is given on request or for distress [[34:29|AIM 6-2-3]]; ask for emergency equipment to stand by [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

activities.title: Reach Flight Service from the chart
activities.intro: Drag each label to the part of the chart symbol it names.

pins.label: Frequency you can use at this RCO
FSS frequency remoted to the VOR site
Controlling FSS for the VOR site

activities.why: Frequencies above the thin line box are remoted to that site, with the controlling FSS named below [[2:26|CUG 26]]. Tell the specialist where you are and which frequency you are listening on [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a2]].

activities.title: True or false: help is available
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Intercept and escort is always available within minutes anywhere in the country.
cards.why: False. Especially at night or in IFR conditions, it depends on how close SAR units with suitable aircraft on alert are [[34:29|AIM 6-2-3]].

cards.s: You may refuse intercept and escort.
cards.why: True. It is the pilot's prerogative [[34:30|AIM 6-2-3c]].

cards.s: SAR coordinators may start an intercept and escort for an urgency condition in unusual circumstances.
At a nontowered airport with ARFF, you call the incident commander on the CTAF or 121.5 MHz.
An FSS answering through a Remote Communications Outlet always knows which outlet you are near, so your call sign is enough.
cards.why: False. Many FSSs transmit on the same frequency at more than one location; give your location and the frequency you expect a reply on [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a2]].

cards.s: Only FSSs, not ARTCCs, alert the search and rescue system about an aircraft in difficulty.
cards.why: False. ARTCCs and FSSs both alert the SAR system when they learn an aircraft is in difficulty, overdue or missing [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]].

activities.title: Minutes and amps
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Night, battery only. Using AFH Figure 18-9, you keep the four wingtip lights, one communications receiver (use 2 amps, the top of its range), the two instrument lights and the fuel indicator. What continuous load is left, in amps?
items.why: 3.00 + 2.00 + 0.60 + 0.40 = 6.00 amps [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. The AFH says what counts as an emergency load depends on things like day or night and VFR or IFR [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

items.q: On a clear day, battery only. Using AFH Figure 18-9, how many amps do you shed by turning off the pitot heat and the four wingtip lights?
Using AFH Figure 18-9, how many amps would the flap motor and both landing lights draw together?
items.why: 13.00 + 17.80 = 30.80 amps [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. The AFH says a 40 amp load might discharge a battery in about 10 or 15 minutes [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

items.q: The AFH example: a 25 amp-hour battery feeding a 5 amp load. About how many hours?
items.why: 25 / 5 = 5 hours, as the AFH states. Do not extend the division to higher loads: at 10 amps the AFH says it might last only 2 hours, not 2.5 [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

activities.title: Late afternoon, low fuel, lost
activities.intro: You are VFR in a Cessna 172, not on flight following, transponder on 1200. After a detour around showers you are unsure of your position. You have about 45 minutes of fuel and the sun is getting low.

steps.s: You are not talking to anyone. Which station does the AIM say you should normally call?
options: The CTAF of your departure airport
The ATC facility responsible for the area you are in, on its assigned frequency from the sectional
Your home FBO on its unicom
No one, until you are sure it is an emergency
steps.why: If you are not receiving services, the station called is normally the air traffic facility in whose area you are operating, on the appropriate assigned frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Doubt about position or fuel is already at least urgency [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

steps.s: While you get ready to call, what does the AIM suggest you do with the airplane if you can?
options: Descend to read town names
Climb, for better communications and radar and DF detection
Slow to minimum speed
Turn off the transponder
steps.why: Climb, if possible, for improved communications and better radar and DF detection [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2a1]].

steps.s: You call the approach frequency from your sectional and hear nothing back. What next?
options: Give up on the radio
Set 7700 and transmit on 121.5 MHz
Set 7600
Switch to the CTAF of your departure airport
steps.why: If you cannot immediately establish communications, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]; 121.5 MHz is available for distress or urgency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. The PHAK gives the same steps for a lost pilot [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

steps.s: A tower answers on 121.5 and finds you on radar. It asks for your fuel remaining. You have about 45 minutes in the tanks, and you had hoped to land with 30 minutes left. What do you say?
options: "One five minutes"
"Four five minutes"
"About six gallons"
"Minimum fuel"
steps.why: Fuel remaining is the approximate number of minutes you can keep flying, with all reserve fuel included [[34:349|P/CG F-6]]; the message element is fuel remaining in minutes [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

steps.s: The tower starts vectoring you to a field 15 miles away. The controller sounds rushed while giving a string of headings and altitudes. What does the AFH say?
options: Turn and climb as fast as you can to keep up
Do not rush into a maneuver that could cost control; it is reasonable to ask the controller to slow down
Ignore the headings and navigate on your own
Squawk 7600 to cut your workload
steps.why: A sense of urgency from the controller reflects normal concern for safety, but do not let it rush you into a maneuver that could cause loss of control; it is reasonable to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].
